title: Sandpapering Our Structural Decay
synopsis: Critiques Australia's misplaced priorities, comparing national outrage over cricket cheating to indifference toward economic decline and squandered natural resources.

content:
There's a peculiar inversion at the heart of Australian public life that I've been struggling to put into words. We reserve our most intense scrutiny for the things that matter least, while the things that matter most proceed almost entirely unexamined.

Consider the Sandpaper affair. For weeks the nation was consumed by the spectacle of cricketers cheating at a game. Inquiries were held. Careers ended. The moral fabric of the country was, we were assured, at stake. Meanwhile the actual structural conditions of Australian life continued their quiet deterioration, noticed by few and addressed by fewer.

I raise it as a contrast rather than to minimise sporting integrity. The contrast illuminates how we allocate collective attention, and the allocation is strange.

The social contract here has become something rather different from what it was. The mythology of mateship survives in our rhetoric while the reality has drifted towards something more extractive. A small cohort floats on salaries above six hundred thousand dollars while the majority experience what can only be described as a contraction in real living standards. Wealth is measured in inflated asset values, and the lived experience of most Australians grows measurably harder each year.

Our political class is among the best compensated on earth. The Prime Minister earns roughly six hundred thousand annually and backbenchers start above two hundred and thirty thousand, figures exceeding what comparable officials receive in nations with far larger economies. I don't begrudge anyone a decent salary. There's something unsettling all the same about a system where those presiding over a national decline are so generously rewarded for it.

The only genuinely effective correction would tie political compensation to the wellbeing of ordinary citizens, so that when the bottom half struggles those at the top feel it too. This will never happen. The thought experiment clarifies things anyway.

**Digging and Shipping**

We sit on extraordinary natural wealth. A fifth of global lithium reserves. A third of the world's rutile. Iron ore, nickel, copper, rare earths. Our approach to this inheritance has been remarkably consistent: dig it up, ship it out raw, buy back the finished products at a premium. Agriculture repeats the pattern, with Australian beef commanding top prices on Shanghai menus while becoming steadily less affordable in suburban supermarkets.

The coal position is the clearest absurdity. We hold some of the world's largest reserves. We export that coal to China, which uses it to power factories manufacturing goods, which we then import at substantial markup. The energy that could have powered Australian manufacturing powers Chinese manufacturing instead, and we pay twice - once in the resource extracted, once in the product bought back. That's structural dependence dressed as economic strategy.

The manufacturing collapse is nearly complete. Twenty-eight percent of GDP in the 1960s down to under six percent today, the lowest in the OECD. We rank 102nd globally in economic complexity, between Bangladesh and Senegal. We can't manufacture an EpiPen. We import ninety percent of our pharmaceuticals and eighty-five percent of our medical devices. When Ford, Holden and Toyota left in 2017 they took a hundred and twenty supplier companies with them, and the tooling and institutional knowledge and trained workforce dispersed.

I think often about Norway. They found oil in 1969 and, instead of treating it as a windfall to spend, established the Government Pension Fund Global. It holds roughly 1.7 trillion dollars today, about 300,000 dollars for every Norwegian, generating returns sufficient to finance national investment while sustaining some of the highest living standards anywhere. We have comparable natural wealth and a sovereign fund holding 230 billion dollars, or 8,800 dollars per Australian. Norway built something durable. We built a housing bubble and called it prosperity.

**Rules That Prevent Rather Than Enable**

The regulatory environment has come to resemble umpiring in modern AFL - well-intentioned in theory and suffocating in practice. Starting a mine, an abattoir or a small business means navigating a bureaucratic labyrinth that defeats everyone except the most determined or best resourced. The impulse to add another rule after every failure has produced a system that prevents things from happening rather than enabling them.

Energy policy represents the most complete failure of imagination. We have endless solar exposure and vast stretches of unpopulated desert, and we could lead the world in photovoltaic deployment, exporting clean energy as readily as we once exported coal. Instead power prices rise while feed-in tariffs fall, and households with rooftop solar earn pennies per kilowatt-hour while retailers post record profits.

Beneath the visible failures sits a quieter one. Our critical digital infrastructure is controlled almost entirely by foreign corporations. Australian business data lives on servers owned by Amazon, Microsoft or Google - American companies under American law. Our payment systems run on foreign networks. The undersea cables connecting us to the internet are operated by foreign entities. We've built an economy that can't function without infrastructure we don't control, and we've done it without any serious national conversation about what that means.

The housing market has inflated past any connection to underlying value. Climate policy remains largely symbolic. Indigenous disadvantage persists through decades of targets and programmes. The National Broadband Network ranks eighty-third globally. Defence research is starved while procurement contracts flow overseas.

And now a transformation in artificial intelligence approaches that will reshape every part of economic life, with no credible national response anywhere in sight.

The consultancy estimates put 1.3 million Australian workers needing new careers by 2030, with a third of the workforce facing displacement - projections assuming capability plateaus, progress stays linear, and there's time to adapt. I believe none of those assumptions.

What I observe is capability doubling every few months, aimed squarely at the jobs that were supposed to be safe. The knowledge work, the analysis, the skilled professional roles. The junior positions that trained the next generation of experts are disappearing, law firms are cutting graduate hiring, accounting practices are shrinking entry-level programmes, and the cognitive ladder previous generations climbed is losing its rungs faster than anyone can climb them.

Our political class still struggles with how the internet works and is manifestly unprepared. The policy response centres on reskilling, as though the challenge were teaching new skills to people who lack them, which misunderstands the disruption entirely. You cannot reskill millions of people into a handful of expert positions, particularly when the remaining positions require capabilities that take years to build.

Education compounds it. The system remains optimised for standardised outcomes and skills being automated at speed - memorisation, calculation, routine analysis - which were valuable and are becoming commodities. We have no serious national conversation about what education means when the traditional pathways to competence are being dismantled underneath it.

**One Thing First**

If I had to choose a single starting point from this whole catalogue, it would be industrial energy price, and I'd choose it for a structural reason rather than an environmental one.

Almost everything else on this list runs downstream of it. Automated manufacturing is, economically, a machine for turning electricity into goods, which means the country with the cheapest industrial power wins that conversion regardless of its wage rates. We have more sun and wind and uranium than nearly anywhere on earth alongside some of the highest industrial electricity costs in the developed world, which may be the strangest fact about this country. Fix that number and the battery plants and datacentres and processing facilities become investable without anyone needing to subsidise them one at a time.

I became a father recently, and Arthur will grow up in this country. He'll inherit a nation that exports its resources and imports its necessities, whose critical infrastructure is controlled by others, whose political class earns among the highest salaries on earth while presiding over a quiet unravelling.

Whether Australia can muddle through in some diminished form isn't really in doubt. It probably can. Whether we're capable of something better is the actual question.

The raw materials are here. The human capital exists. What seems to be missing is any political will to do more than manage decline while protecting the people who benefit from the current arrangements. My son deserves leaders prepared to build rather than maintain monuments to past failures, and I suspect most Australians feel something similar. The gap between what we could be and what we're choosing to be widens every year, and some questions, deferred long enough, answer themselves.
